transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-01 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Aisha (Redwood SE), Priya (Aurelia PM), Sam (Aurelia Infra), Jon (Aurelia SRE), Mei (Aurelia ML Eng)

Summary (auto): SE walked through knobs to optimize throughput: continuous batching, scheduler window, max_num_seqs, token caps, and KV cache behaviors. Discussed quantization tradeoffs and VPC/on-prem limits.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for carving out time, quick intros then we'll jump into throughput tuning. Carlos is going to lead the tech part.
[00:18] Priya (Aurelia): thanks, yes we want to reduce p99 for generation and increase overall TPS for our chat pipeline. we've got spikes at EOD and our current infra is hitting queuing.
[00:35] Carlos (Redwood): great; quick callout on what we'll cover — continuous batching, scheduler knobs like scheduling window and max_num_seqs, token limits per request, kv cache warmup and quantization effects. we'll also talk about VPC/on-prem constraints.
[00:50] Mei (Aurelia): quick note — our average request is 120 tokens, tail up to 1.2k on long docs, and we do a lot of short-chat traffic too.
[01:05] Carlos (Redwood): perfect, that's the kind of distribution we tuned for. ok first: continuous batching. the idea is we keep a small window and continuously fill batches instead of waiting for fixed batch sizes. helps throughput without big latency hit if set correctly.
[01:30] Jon (Aurelia): can you quantify "small window"? we've tried a 50ms window and saw some request accumulation causing p95 blips.
[01:43] Carlos (Redwood): sure — typical windows we recommend are 10-40ms for low-latency use cases; 50-100ms if you care more about raw throughput. but it's workload dependent. for your mix (many 120-token requests) a 20-30ms window with adaptive overflow works well.
[02:05] Priya (Aurelia): adaptive overflow?
[02:09] Carlos (Redwood): yeah, the scheduler can be set to let a request overflow into next batch if it's waiting too long, or force-send if it hits max latency. Redwood's scheduler has knobs: scheduling_window_ms, max_batch_size, max_num_seqs (per GPU), and token_cap_per_batch.
[02:30] Priya: we've seen sometimes large requests block small ones, any best practice there?
[02:36] Carlos: set token limits and seq bucketing. one approach: cap tokens-per-request at a soft limit (e.g., 1k) and set max_num_seqs to prefer more shorter sequences per batch. For example on A100 80GB we often use max_num_seqs=16-32 for 512-token avg, but if you have many short chats you can bump to 64. this reduces per-token kernel overhead.
[03:05] Sam: how does kv cache affect batching? when users do multi-turn we cache KV but we see inconsistent warmup.
[03:15] Aisha (Redwood): good question — KV cache warmup matters for latency on resumed contexts. if KV cache is cold, first resumed request pays overhead. we recommend prefix caching and keeping hot contexts pinned for frequent users. also, continuous batching should prefer requests with warmed caches where possible — a scheduler policy we can share.
[03:36] Mei: any gotchas with quantization? we tried 4-bit and saw occasional quality drift.
[03:43] Carlos: quantization yields cost/throughput wins but can change sample quality; use Redwood Optimize suggestions: per-workload evals and fallback to fp16 for critical flows. Also 4-bit int8-like schemes have faster kernels but watch for longer tail latency on some ops if kernel selection falls back.
[04:10] Jon: when you mention kernel selection fallback, does that impact our p99?
[04:15] Carlos: yes — if the runtime picks a non-optimized kernel because of a sequence length or kv-cache pattern, you'll see higher p99. we instrument kernel selection; the console can show per-token kernel timings.
[04:35] Priya: what about max_num_seqs knob again, practical numbers for our infra (we're on 8xA100-ish dedicated)?
[04:44] Carlos: for 8xA100 dedicated, start with max_num_seqs=32, scheduling_window=25ms, max_batch_size tuned to GPU memory. also enable batch packing by seq length bucket. Run bench: adjust upward if avg seq length < 256. we'll supply a test script.
[05:05] Priya: token caps per batch?
[05:08] Carlos: set token_cap_per_batch to constrain total tokens per batch (e.g., 16k tokens) to avoid OOM from few long seqs filling memory. combined with per-request token_limit this prevents long requests from starving the batch.
[05:30] Maya: we also recommend per-route policies: real-time chat route vs background summarization route can have different knobs — keep chat with tighter windows.
[05:45] Sam: VPC/on-prem — any limitations for continuous batching or scheduler knobs when running Private?
[05:51] Carlos: functionally it's the same. main differences are networking latency to control plane and storage for KV cache. on-prem you manage node leases; you may want to set slightly larger scheduling windows if your intra-node latency is variable. also ensure the control-plane heartbeat is healthy or batch pacing can be off.
[06:15] Mei: do we need special kernel builds for private?
[06:20] Carlos: we provide optimized runtime packages for on-prem. if you're air-gapped we can ship an installer. kernel selection is still runtime-driven. sometimes customers with older CUDA stacks see different perf; we document recommended CUDA/cuDNN versions.
[06:36] Priya: can we see a real benchmark example?
[06:40] Carlos: yes I'll walk through a quick example — baseline: no continuous batching, max_batch_size 8, max_num_seqs 8 -> 120 TPS, p95 420ms. With continuous batching at 25ms, max_num_seqs 32, token_cap 16k -> 320 TPS, p95 260ms, p99 improved too in many cases. these are illustrative for a 512-token average workload.
[07:12] Jon: that's a big uplift. what's the tail behavior for mixed short+long?
[07:17] Carlos: mixed workloads require bucketing and preemptive sending for long tails. you can classify requests at ingress (short vs long) and route to different queue priorities. Redwood supports per-route scheduler policies.
[07:35] Mei: any suggestions around caching TTLs?
[07:38] Aisha: a short TTL for ephemeral sessions (e.g., 5-15 minutes) and sticky caching for power users. also use prefix caching for common prompts to avoid recompute.
[07:50] Priya: are there tradeoffs between increasing max_num_seqs and latency jitter?
[07:55] Carlos: yes — larger max_num_seqs increases throughput but can increase latency for first-in requests if the scheduler waits to fill batch. that's why scheduling_window_ms and adaptive overflow are important. tune until you hit acceptable p95.
[08:12] Sam: about metrics — what to monitor?
[08:15] Carlos: tokens/sec, req/sec, avg batch size, scheduling_wait_ms, kernel_fallback_count, kv_cache_hit_ratio, per-model p95/p99 latency. Redwood Console exposes these.
[08:33] Priya: ok let's talk concrete bench plan — we can supply prompt distribution and run your script?
[08:38] Maya: yes we'll provide bench script and a spreadsheet to collect runs. please include your seq length histogram.
[08:48] Mei: do you support simultaneous multi-model routing (fallback to smaller model on heavy load)?
[08:54] Carlos: yes we have routing policies to fallback to cheaper/quantized variants. there's also automatic degrade paths to keep SLOs.
[09:05] Jon: any security implications for KV cache and persistence?
[09:10] Aisha: KV cache can be kept in-memory only for privacy. for Private deployments you can control persistence and KMS for any saved artifacts. Audit logs and RBAC are available.
[09:25] Priya: ok next, let's commit to a run: what config will you try first?
[09:29] Carlos: we'll try scheduling_window_ms=25, max_num_seqs=32, token_cap_per_batch=16000, adaptive_overflow=true, enable continuous batching. We'll run 3 runs: baseline, medium, aggressive.
[09:44] Priya: timeline?
[09:45] Maya: we can have data back in ~5 business days once you send prompt set and grant access to test S3.
[09:52] Sam: we'll get that over by Tuesday.
[09:55] Maya: perfect. action items recap in the doc.
[10:00] Carlos: one more note — quantization fallback rules: run evals on your critical prompts; if 4-bit shows drift above 1-2% delta on metrics, keep fp16 for that route. our Optimize tool can do these checks automatically.
[10:20] Priya: good to know. Any recommendation on logging/tracing for kernel fallback?
[10:25] Carlos: enable kernel_trace in runtime and sample traces for p99 events. Console collects aggregate kernel fallback counts.
[10:35] Mei: for on-prem pilot, we'll need an installer and recommended CUDA versions.
[10:39] Aisha: we'll share an on-prem checklist and installer link.
[10:45] Jon: last question — do you have prescriptive defaults for small teams vs enterprise?
[10:50] Maya: yes small teams default to lower max_num_seqs and shorter windows to favor latency; enterprise/Dedicated can push throughput knobs. We'll include default profiles in the playbook.
[11:05] Priya: great thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[11:09] Maya: thanks — we'll follow up with configs and bench sheet.

References:
